title: ★ X Once Again Marks the Spot
content:
Upon taking the CEO helm last month, John Ternus began tweeting on X. He tweeted “hello”, posted an iPhone event eve teaser and then a promo video for the new products, celebrated Apple’s plethora of wins at the Emmys and launch day on Fifth Avenue, and commemorated the anniversary of Steve Jobs’s death.

X is the only place these posts go. Same for Greg Joswiak’s account. Lighthearted stuff too, like Cook “introducing” Ternus to Pikachu back in August. You may not like it that X has re-found its footing under Elon Musk’s ownership, but it has. I’m citing Apple executives here but they’re far from alone. There are hundreds of interesting people and accounts I follow that post on X very regularly and do not post anywhere else at all. As a word nerd I love Merriam-Webster’s account — fun, clever, smart posts every day. That’s just one example among hundreds. Here’s another. Fascinating new apps are being shown and discussed on X and nowhere else.

[Update: I stand corrected — Merriam-Webster does have an account on Bluesky. It contains, most, but not all, of the items they post to X. They’ve posted 34 original new tweets on X so far in October; only 10 on Bluesky. Plus on X they’ve chimed in with 11 clever and/or informative retweets from other accounts, including one from those notorious fascists at Sesame Street; there are zero of those on Blueksy. So while I regret the error of implying that Merriam-Webster posts exclusively on X, the 45-10 count for October to date proves my point just as well.]

I see more interesting posts on X than I do on Threads, Bluesky, and Mastodon combined. I wish that weren’t so but it is. Most people don’t want to think about politics so they don’t. Those people, when they want to participate in a Twitter-like social network, go to X.

And I can’t blame anyone. The only network that compares to X, size-wise, is Threads — but Threads’s algorithm is weirder than X’s now, and the content I see there is relatively boring. My Threads timeline is full of engagement bait without being engaging. And if you want to judge a platform by its owner, “I’m grossed out and/or appalled by Elon Musk so I’m going to Mark Zuckerberg’s joint” isn’t a way to avoid being grossed out and/or appalled by the owner. Bluesky and Mastodon are too small for most people to care about — and, worse, they are the networks where politics are, in my experience, unavoidable. You can have a discussion about cool new use cases and tools for AI on X and people just discuss the tools and use cases. On Bluesky and Mastodon it’s difficult to have such discussions without arguments from people who (a) believe all use of AI is unethical, and (b) will shove their viewpoints into your replies.

The culture on X today is remarkably friendly and inclusive. It is a cheerful place. That cheerfulness is another differentiator. If you believe the world is falling apart and doomed only to get worse, that our obvious and real problems cannot be surmounted, X is not the platform for you. If you think the world is full of fun and amazing people and things, that humanity’s defining feature is our collective ability to solve any problem, that the only time better to be alive than today is tomorrow, it might be.

If you have stayed away, or even just mostly away, from X for years and then come back, people just say things like “Hey, glad you’re back!” On the other networks, especially Mastodon, they tell you you’re “feeding Nazis” — by going to the platform where Tim Cook posts Pikachu videos. These people have either lost their minds or refuse to check their prior assumptions. (Most of the ones who chime in about it publicly are the lost-their-minds types.)

But the bigger problem is that there’s little action on Bluesky or, especially, Mastodon. There’s a lot of activity on Threads, but little action. There is action on X. I’ve said for years that Mastodon is my favorite of the bunch and in a way it still is, but really that’s because when I go there I don’t have to be diligent to avoid wasting time. I avoid wasting time on Mastodon because there’s so little of interest to see. That’s a feature — for me — but it certainly isn’t what most people are looking for in a Twitter-like posting platform. They want action. The action is on X.

Without any fanfare — perhaps to avoid his ire — X has de-Musked its algorithm. I stopped visiting at all when the algorithm there was putting Musk’s own tweets into my timeline, every time I checked, despite the fact that I never followed him. But they don’t do that anymore. I don’t see much politics of any kind in my timeline, and what I do see is from accounts I chose to follow. I see tech (including a lot of interesting breaking news), sports (including a lot of interesting videos and stats), and stupid stuff that’s actually funny. My only problem with X now is that I do have to pay attention to avoid wasting time when I visit.

Plus, in addition to the tweets, there are now many interesting people using X to post entire essays and blog posts. I wish that weren’t so, for multiple reasons (e.g., no RSS). But it is so.

If you returned from exile on a desert island and took a look at X today for the first time in a year, you might reasonably guess that Elon Musk got bored and sold it while you were away. I do think he got bored micromanaging it, but the rank muskiness that permeated the platform after he took over is — for now, at least — gone.

title: Why I Get Bored
content:
For me, boredom is just a signal. It means I've hit a roadblock and my brain is trying to convince me not to go any further. "Give up. This sucks anyway. Why are you still wasting your time on this silly thing?"

That's how I feel when I do things I'm really bad at. I think I'm not good at making YouTube videos. Whenever I think of a subject I find really exciting, I start writing, record a first pass, and then load DaVinci Resolve.

With my current schedule, job, family, and responsibilities, I've found that it takes me a whole week to polish three minutes of video. That means I hear the same material I wrote and recorded over and over until it becomes completely boring. After a few weeks, I lose interest in the subject and have no motivation to finish it.

But I think that's just an excuse I tell myself. I like the videos I've managed to complete. I wish I could change some parts, but I still like the final product. It's just that the process gets in the way, and it does so because I have no expertise in making videos. But then again, I always go back to my trusted method: if you're bad at something, do it at least a hundred times before you decide to give up.

We all suck at the beginning, and we're in no position to judge a craft until we've practiced it enough to love it or hate it. So here's to another attempt. I'll be publishing videos in the coming weeks. The first one will be just a minute long, the second will be two minutes long, the third... you get the gist. Hope you enjoy it.

title: One way of thinking about access specifiers in C++/WinRT implementation types
content:
In C++/WinRT, Windows Runtime classes are exposed to the outside world through the projection, but internally they are represented by their implementation type. Since the outside world sees only the projection, implementation types are visible only to the module that produced them.

This realization lets you reinterpret the C++ access specifiers for C++/WinRT implementation types.

Declared on
implementation as		 C# and C++/CX
equivalent		 Accessible to
implemented interface public Anyone
public internal Code in the same module
protected protected Code in derived classes
private private Code in the same class

In code:

struct Widget : winrt::implements<Widget, IStringable>
{
public:
    // This is a member of IStringable,
    // so it is accessible to anyone.
    winrt::hstring ToString();

    // This does not implement any member from IStringable,
    // so it is accessible to other code in the same module.
    void Recolor(winrt::Windows::UI::Color newColor);

protected:
    // Accessible to implementation classes that derive from Widget.
    void Reverse();

private:
    // Accessible only to Widget itself.
    void Reset();
};

Note that if you are implementing a runtime class, then C++/WinRT autogenerates a template for you that auto-declares all of the declared interfaces of that class.

// Widget.idl

namespace Contoso
{
    runtimeclass Widget : Windows.Foundation.IStringable
    {
        String Name{ get; };
        void Toggle();
    }
}

The IDL compiler autogenerates an interface IWidget with a property Name and a method Toggle().

// implementation
namespace winrt::Contoso
{
    struct Widget : WidgetT<Widget>
    {
        ⟦ ... ⟧
    };
}

The WidgetT<Widget> expands to implements<Widget, IWidget, Windows::Foundation::IStringable> because those are the interfaces declared by the IDL file.

The post One way of thinking about access specifiers in C++/WinRT implementation types appeared first on The Old New Thing.
description: Mapping them to concepts from C# and the now-defunct C++/CX. The post One way of thinking about access specifiers in C++/WinRT implementation types appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: Just say no to OpenAI and Anthropic
content:
I recently read End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. It's an excellent book and I highly recommend that everyone read it. Tech oligarchs make up an important component of the end-times-fascist coalition. One thing that stood out to me, as a software and security engineer who finds LLMs to be extremely powerful, is that the American frontier labs are run by unhinged lunatics who genuinely believe they're creating the Machine God, that they're fine with burning down the world to bring about AGI, and that they believe with religious fervor that they're the only ones smart enough to safely control it. I already kind of knew this, but this book really made it sink in.

As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they're not. They're not the only companies doing this work. In fact, a lot of the open weight models are just about as good as the latest ChatGPT and Claude models, including for incredibly complex tasks like vulnerability research.

Unlike models from OpenAI and Anthropic, open weight models have major advantages:

  • It's possible to run them privately on your own hardware (if you can somehow get a computer with enough RAM)
  • You can use a provider like Tinfoil that relies on secure enclaves to run them privately (I talk about this in a bit more detail below)
  • If privacy isn't a huge concern, you can use any number of other providers, some of them quite affordable, and it's easy to switch so you're not locked into a single evil vendor
  • You can still use powerful LLMs without financially supporting deranged oligarchs who gamble with life on Earth so that they can always remain in power

ChatGPT and Claude will never be private

These companies only offer closed versions of their powerful models (despite the word "open" in "OpenAI"). You pay them for chat and/or API access, and they are allowed to look at everything you do.

They offer a checkbox so you can opt out of them using your data for training, but your chat sessions still aren't private. They have access to it all. They can look at it, share it with governments or companies, or do whatever they want. It's possible, likely even, that they won't use it for training if you've opted out, at least not right now. But do you really trust that long-term? Have they done anything to make anyone believe that they respect people's data?

OpenAI and Anthropic are corporate gatekeepers

Their models have strict guardrails, as anyone who's tried to use them for anything cybersecurity-related has no doubt noticed.

Every session has a cop agent reading your transcript over your shoulder, making sure you're not using it for hacking. If it thinks you might be, the cop agent stops your session from continuing. It's very strict, and false positives happen all the time. Of course, not everyone has the cop watching them.

Some people get access to the models with looser restrictions or with none at all. OpenAI has Trusted Access for Cyber and Anthropic has the Cyber Verification Program. To gain access to more capable, less policed versions of their models, individuals and companies need to apply and be approved by OpenAI and Anthropic. A lot of US cybersecurity companies get access. Almost certainly US military contractors do too, and probably any parts of the US government that want it.

While there's some merit in restricting powerful models, handing the ultimate power to decide who gets access to them to Sam Altman and Dario Amodei – with consultation from the Trump Administration, of course – is a terrible, undemocratic idea.

I think a better approach is to simply not put yourself in a situation where you rely on ChatGPT or Claude. Instead of begging corporate overlords for privileged access, it's better to spend your time figuring out how to get models like GLM-5.3 to meet your needs. And it's not hard. These models are good, with the added benefit that they don't have a cop watching over your shoulder!

Open weight models are impressive

So far, open weight models seem to be about four months behind the fancy proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Four months is nothing.

I'm extremely impressed right now with GLM-5.3. There's plenty of data and benchmarks out there, but my vibes-based opinion from using it is that it's basically on par with Claude Opus 5.5 for software engineering.

I'm also impressed with GLM-5.3-Flash. This is similar to Claude Opus 4.8. It's much smaller and cheaper than GLM-5.3, and still incredibly capable. It's also actually feasible for an individual person to get hardware to run it, like if you can one day get your hands on a Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM.

GLM models are made by a Chinese company called Z.ai. While the models are impressive, I don't recommend making an account directly with Z.ai or sending them any of your data. Their coding harness ZCode (their version of Claude Code) was recently caught silently uploading local source code repos and sending them back to Alibaba Cloud without consent. Also, it's safe to assume that Chinese companies will share any data you provide to them with the Chinese government.

Other open weight models from Chinese companies that are impressive include the DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi families of models. It's perfectly fine, safe, and secure to use these open weight models. Just don't trust the companies themselves with your chat sessions.

Another frontier AI lab worth a look is Mistral. As a French company, it's the only big player that's not Chinese or American. They just released an open weight frontier model called Mistral Large 4, aka Le Chonk. I think it's quite a bit more reasonable to trust Mistral with your data compared to the Chinese or American companies.

Private inference with Tinfoil or Maple AI

It's possible to have private AI, even without hosting it locally yourself, using secure enclaves. These aren't perfect, but I do think they provide a very meaningful difference in privacy compared to the status quo mode, which is "the provider can access everything with no restrictions."

The company that's doing the most work here is Tinfoil. If you want to learn the details, read their docs on secure enclaves and remote attestation. Another company doing this is Maple AI – although, technically, Maple uses Tinfoil for inference in the background.

Both Tinfoil and Maple are good options. Tinfoil is cheaper, but Maple is more consumer-focused.

If you want a ChatGPT-like experience, where you can talk to a chatbot, have it look stuff up for you on the internet, give it access to docs to read or do stuff with, access it in a mobile app, etc., then I'd go with Maple. There's a small free plan and a Pro plan that costs $20/month.

If you want to do real agentic coding tasks like software engineering, reverse engineering, malware analysis, CTFs or pen tests, etc., then you should use Tinfoil instead. They charge by the token for private inference, so no monthly plan. GLM-5.3 currently costs $1.80 per 1M input tokens, $0.80 per 1M cached tokens, and $5.75 per 1M output tokens. You can use significantly fewer tokens if you choose the "low" reasoning level, and it's still very impressive.

Inference without the privacy

If you don't want to pay a premium for private inference from Tinfoil or Maple, but you still want to free yourself from OpenAI and Anthropic, there are tons of less-private options that are also very cheap.

One that I've been playing with is OpenCode Go. It costs $10/month for more than $10 worth of credits. This is an inference router, which basically means your API queries do something like this: your computer -> OpenCode Go API -> the actual inference provider. This means that both OpenCode Go and whatever backend provider they're using will have access to your session data. That said, the privacy section of their docs promises which models data won't be used for training (most of them) and what the data retention is (zero days for most, including all the GLM, Qwen, Kimi, and DeepSeek models). Of course, it's just a promise. Nothing technical guarantees it.

There are plenty of other cheap options out there for non-private inference, if you just want to experiment with powerful open weight models.

How I'm using these models

I've been using both Tinfoil and OpenCode Go, configured with my current harness of choice, OpenCode. I've been mostly using GLM-5.3 on low reasoning, with great results. (Things change so quickly with the open weight models, who knows what will be best six months from now.)

I use OpenCode Go inference for completely public work, like when I'm implementing something that's already open source.

I use Tinfoil for everything else.

I've only just started working this way, but so far, I think the open weight models can easily completely replace my use of ChatGPT and Claude, at a comparable or cheaper price, with the added benefit that they're far more private and there are far fewer guardrails.
